Microsoft and Adobe are suspended from H-1B visa program, with Vance accusing the tech giants of fraud
item.description:
Microsoft and Adobe have been suspended from the H-1B visa program, Vice President JD Vance announced Thursday, amid accusations that they and other companies have extensively abused the system to hire cheaper labor.

“This is a great day for American workers, because we are taking some very concrete actions to cut down on some of the H-1B and J-1 visa fraud that we’ve been tracking over the past several months,” Vance said at a Thursday morning press conference.

Microsoft and Adobe did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The J-1 visa is for foreign students, teachers, researchers and a few other visitor categories. The H-1B program allows companies to hire nonimmigrant foreign workers for roles that require specialized knowledge when they can’t be filled by the U.S. workforce.

Vance said the latter program has become “rife with fraud over the last several years—probably the last several decades.”

Rather than use H-1B visas for their intended purpose, he said, companies and outsourcing firms are using it to replace American workers “with what is effectively foreign indentured servants,” who are “being mistreated by their employers and being used to undercut the wages of American workers.”

Broader Trump crackdown

The announcements follow an executive order in September that announced a review of the program’s application data, alleging “large-scale, systematic abuse” by companies.

The order—which comes from an administration whose attacks on science and research have been documented extensively—also characterized the abuse as a national security threat for discouraging Americans from “pursuing careers in science and technology.” 

The Trump administration has taken other actions to rein in H-1B visas, including last year’s announcement of a $100,000 fee for new applications, causing backlash and legal challenges.

Roughly 400,000 H-1B visas were approved in 2024, according to Pew Research, more than double the number approved in 2000.

Tech companies singled out

Vance said that no company has abused the program more than Microsoft, which he said laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from “6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.”

The secretary of Labor, Keith Sonderling, also announced that the program would no longer take applications from several major outsourcing firms, which supply companies with foreign candidates.

The U.S. tech industry relies heavily on H-1B workers, who earn on average 16% less than their American counterparts, according to a National Bureau of Economic Research paper.

In the 2024 fiscal year, 64% of H-1B visa recipients worked in computer-related occupations, according to federal data.

The H-1B program “is now the major pathway for employment-based immigrants to enter and stay in the United States,” according to a study published in International Migration Review this year, creating a power imbalance between employers and migrant workers.

Criticism across party lines

Criticism of the H-1B program has previously caused infighting among Trump’s associates, and crossed party lines.

Bernie Sanders said last year that he disagrees with claims by Elon Musk and other tech titans that the program is vital due to a scarcity of highly-skilled American workers.

The independent senator from Vermont said that corporations will lay off American workers while hiring new H-1B workers, even though U.S. Census data indicates that millions of Americans with advanced STEM degrees are not employed in their field.

“The cheaper the labor they hire, the more money the billionaires make,” Sanders said.

At the press conference, Vance said the government also sees “a lot of J-1 visa fraud,” naming nine universities “that we believe merit an investigation,” claiming they employ J-1 visa students to work on federally funded grants at a rate much higher than the national average.

“We cannot allow visa programs that were designed to ensure that American corporations had access to the best and the brightest to use them to undercut the wages of American workers,” Vance said.

“Now, it’s one thing if you want to bring in a person like Elon Musk,” he added. “Obviously, if that person wants to come in and build something great in the United States of America, we support that.”

Musk, who immigrated from South Africa, has previously defended the H-1B program, vowing that “I will go to war on this issue.”

He has held both J-1 and H-1B visas, and has been accused of violating the terms of the former, which he has denied. His company, Tesla, is also facing a class action lawsuit that alleges it of having a “systematic preference” for hiring H-1B visa holders and disproportionately firing U.S. citizens.

Shares of Microsoft Corporation (Nasdaq: MSFT) fell after the announcement on Thursday, closing 1.35% lower. But the stock was up about 1% in premarket trading on Friday as of this writing.

Adobe Inc (Nasdaq: ADBE) stock was up 3.56% on Thursday despite the announcement.

item.title: The more Putin escalates his attacks on Europe, the more Europe should support Ukraine | Timothy Garton Ash
item.description:
Moscow’s imperialist strongman believes decadent European democracies can be cowed. Our job is to prove him wrong

Vladimir Putin is escalating both his full-scale war against Ukraine and his shadow war against the rest of Europe. His main purpose in the shadow one is to break European support for Ukraine so he can subjugate that country, something he regards as existential for Russia’s future and his own. While we in the rest of Europe must prepare as best we can to defend ourselves against every kind of hybrid attack, the central thrust of our response should be to redouble our support for Ukraine. Ukraine is his main target. It’s there, and only there, not in a contest of a thousand hybrid pinpricks, that Putin’s Russia can in a meaningful sense be defeated and deterred.

In a powerful new book, Warum Russland nicht aufhören wird (Why Russia Won’t Stop), the German historian Martin Schulze Wessel shows how Putin’s policy fits into a much older Russian tradition of territorial expansionism and striving for hegemony, combined with a religiously infused imperial ideology. He reminds us that in 2016 Putin said “Russia’s frontier ends nowhere” and in 2025, “wherever the boot of a Russian soldier steps, that is ours”. West Europeans, fondly imagining that we have consigned such brute territorial imperialism to the dustbin of history, tend to think there must be some other explanation (eg something we did “wrong”, like the eastward expansion of Nato). Finns, Estonians and Poles know better. Despite Russia’s weaknesses, the author concludes, it is “the most dangerous country in the world”. Some in Asia might question that large claim, but certainly Russia is the most dangerous country for Europe.

item.title: Riyadh airport hit by fresh Houthi strike day after deadly attack
item.description:
A fresh Houthi strike hit Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday, a day after another attack claimed by the Yemeni group killed at least a dozen people and forced authorities to suspend operations at the facility.

Saturday’s attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, was a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognised government against the Houthis.

The group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the last 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom’s transit hubs, calling them “a theatre of operations for our forces”.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group “carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones”.

Saree said they targeted the Riyadh airport multiple times, as well as the Dammam airport and two facilities belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco.

Hours later, the Saudi coalition fighting the group reported that a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport, sparking a fire. Air defences also intercepted a missile nearby, it added.

The civil aviation authority said the attack caused an unspecified number of injuries, and that a damage assessment was underway.

AFP journalists and locals reported hearing the sound of multiple blasts in the Saudi capital on Sunday.

“The birds went into a frenzy after the sound. The whole house shook,” said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighbourhood in the north of the city.

‘Full-fledged war crime’

The Houthis have stepped up their attacks on the Riyadh airport — where three people were also killed on Thursday — as well as on other key targets in the world’s top crude oil exporter.

And although Saudi Arabia has poured billions into its military, Houthi attacks continue to slip through.

“Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves against Houthi attacks,” said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University.

The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday’s attack a “full-fledged war crime” and vowed to “respond decisively”.

Houthi media reported two Saudi strikes in Yemen’s Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate on Sunday.

Saturday’s attack drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders around the world, including US President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose country does not have diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, also denounced the “horrific terrorist attack”.

Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed, the civil aviation authority said, with 309 wounded.

The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia also said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded the day before.

A Riyadh-based Western diplomat told AFP the official number of injured may not give a full picture, as it did not appear to include those with minor wounds.

Operations suspended

Authorities suspended operations at the airport into Sunday, a senior aviation source said, with air traffic monitor Flightradar24 saying the closure was extended until 21:00 GMT (2am PKT on Monday).

A second aviation source confirmed the halt in operations “until further notice”, adding radar and communications equipment was damaged and runways needed to be assessed.

Witnesses to Saturday’s strike described chaos in the aftermath.

“People who were in Terminal 3 started running towards us,” a 32-year-old Riyadh resident told AFP.

“Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood.”

The attack prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors, a medical source said.

The US, Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh airport, while Australia urged its citizens on Sunday to stay indoors altogether and “shelter in place”.

The Houthis also claimed to have targeted the Dammam airport, whose official website on Sunday showed many flights — both departures and arrivals — were delayed.

‘Rewrite the rules’

Saturday’s airport strike, on the eve of Saudi Arabia’s high-profile convention and entertainment season, was the deadliest attack in the kingdom since a 2015 suicide bombing.

With the summer heat subsiding, October also usually marks the beginning of the high season for Umrah pilgrims, with millions of Muslims from across the world flocking to Makkah.

Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.

Ottawa University’s Juneau said the Houthis now “want to rewrite the rules of the game”.

“They want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them,” he said.

“So if their airport in Sanaa has to be closed because of the Saudi air embargo, they want to do the same thing to Saudi Arabia.”

On the ground in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing in their counter-offensive against the Houthis around the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping route, military sources said on Saturday.

The Houthis claimed to have repelled them.

Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

item.title: Steve Jones obituary
item.description:
My friend Steve Jones, who has died aged 77, had a working life devoted to humanitarian causes, with a particular focus on Bangladesh and India. In retirement he then dedicated a sizeable portion of his time to charity work, helping people with the lung disease pulmonary fibrosis get the help and treatment they needed.

Steve was born in London to John and Lettie, who were both teachers and shared the surname Jones. After secondary school in Crawley, West Sussex, he studied geography at Bristol University, worked for a short time as an economist for a company that became part of British Airways and then embarked on further studies at Cambridge University, where he gained a certificate in anthropology and began a PhD.

item.title: KP Governor's Rule: An emergency in the street and state
item.description:
Back in 2024, the political future of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and perhaps of Pakistan itself, looked like a coin toss. There were two broad possibilities. One was a grand political settlement, perhaps involving a period of exile for Imran Khan, with the United Kingdom replacing Saudi Arabia as the preferred destination. The other was the eventual termination of the last PTI provincial government through constitutional intervention. One of these possibilities has now materialised.

There was a third option but this was not the 1990s when you could break a party with defections as its leader served time. No, political loyalties have not surged since, we just have tighter rules for turncoats. This gambit would not have worked in KP anyway. Floor crossing can’t be engineered when there has been a landslide.

What we did not know back then was how the PTI government in KP could be dislodged when push came to shove. Indeed, only one of these options has come to pass two years later. The federal government has declared an emergency and Governor’s Rule. There are reports that Chief Minister Sohail Afridi has been arrested. The justification is a law-and-order situation, terrorism and the breakdown in negotiations with the government.

The constitutional justification for federal intervention must be distinguished from its political rationale. Articles 232 and 234 provide extraordinary powers in different circumstances, and their invocation is subject to procedural requirements and limitations. A deterioration in security is an important consideration, but it does not automatically establish that constitutional government has become impossible.

There is also the question of consistency. Balochistan, immediately south and southwest of KP, has experienced its own severe deterioration in security since the 2024 elections. The two provinces face different insurgencies and different political circumstances, but the comparison is unavoidable. If terrorism alone establishes the necessity for extraordinary intervention, why is the constitutional response different in Balochistan?

This does not mean the security challenges in KP are imaginary, or that the provincial government bears no responsibility for its response. It means that the justification for governor’s rule must explain something more specific than the existence of terrorism. It must establish why the existing constitutional machinery could no longer deal with it.

There is, however, another security crisis that helps explain the political context of this decision. It began in 2023, and its protagonists were not militants.

May 9, 2023

May 9 remains consequential for Pakistan’s establishment in ways that subsequent and more lethal security incidents have not been. The attacks on military installations following Imran Khan’s arrest challenged assumptions about the relationship between the military and sections of the public that had traditionally been regarded as politically sympathetic to it.

Since the Arab Spring began in 2010, Pakistan’s security establishment had reason to contemplate the possibility that mass mobilisation might produce consequences beyond the capacity of conventional political management. Pakistan had different institutions, a different political history and a military with a different relationship to the state, especially compared to say Egypt. The spectacle of governments losing control of public spaces, and sometimes their own institutions, had become part of the political imagination of the region.

May 9 tested a version of that fear. The subsequent response suggested that the state possessed a greater capacity to suppress political mobilisation than PTI had anticipated. Arrests, prosecutions, restrictions on political activity and the disruption of party organisation altered the costs of confrontation. A serious underestimation had come to pass.

The implications were particularly significant in Punjab. Although the May 9 incidents were concentrated in several parts of Punjab and KP, the attacks in Lahore carried considerable symbolic weight. A city long associated with the military’s institutional presence and political influence had witnessed an extraordinary breach.

The state’s subsequent response changed the political environment in Punjab. Whatever the underlying level of support for PTI, public participation in confrontational politics became a much more consequential personal decision. The rules of political mobilisation had changed.

Against this background, PTI’s victory in KP in February 2024 was an enormous morale booster. Despite the imprisonment of Imran Khan, the loss of its electoral symbol and substantial impediments to electioneering, the party demonstrated that its electoral appeal remained formidable. KP supplied PTI with something it had lost elsewhere: an elected government, an institutional base and a territory from which to organise its politics, but it also inherited the unresolved strategic problem of May 9.

The failures of 2024

If there was uncertainty about PTI’s intended response, its choice of chief minister provided an early indication. Ali Amin Gandapur was a combative political figure, selected at a time when the party wanted to confront the federal government and demonstrate that its capacity for street mobilisation had survived. The threat of protest was that it would halt the business of the state.

He attempted to deliver on that expectation. In October and November 2024, PTI organised major efforts to reach Islamabad’s D-Chowk, the second involving Bushra Bibi. Both ended in retreats, and the November confrontation involved casualties, injuries and a disputed account of the security operation: however, the consequences went beyond the failure to occupy a public square.

For the federal government, the confrontations demonstrated that the capital could be defended against a determined political mobilisation. For PTI, they exposed the distance between the ability to assemble supporters and the ability to sustain a confrontation against a state willing to escalate.

Gandapur too suffered the burden of May 9. The people in Punjab were no longer willing to protest in the same way after being subjected to preemptive arrests and controls. KP’s electorate were tired as well, but the effort it made was rewarded with abandonment and careless endangerment when the party leadership abruptly left both protests in late 2024. A year later, CM Gandapur was asked to resign.

There was also resentment over the comparatively limited mobilisation from Punjab. Workers from KP were being asked to shoulder risks that supporters elsewhere were either unwilling or unable to assume.

The official explanation for Gandapur’s resignation centred on the deteriorating security situation and disagreements over counterterrorism policy, but the failures of 2024 had already weakened his political standing. The larger problem survived his departure. PTI’s electoral mandate in KP remained substantial, but its capacity to convert that mandate into sustained national mobilisation was less certain. Electoral popularity and street power are different political assets. A party can retain the overwhelming loyalty of its voters while finding that those same voters are unwilling to risk arrest, injury or death in repeated attempts at confrontation. That distinction is central to the present crisis.

It is entirely possible that a large proportion of KP’s electorate would vote for PTI again in 2029. That does not establish that the same electorate will respond to every call for another march on Islamabad. The failures of 2024, the disappointment with the leadership and the personal costs of confrontation have changed the calculation for at least some of its supporters.

Yet PTI has frequently negotiated as though the political circumstances of 2014 still prevail, and every neighbourhood can be mobilised on command. The risk is that the party mistakes enduring loyalty to Imran Khan for an unlimited willingness to undertake increasingly costly political action. Its strategy has become difficult to revise, partly because the organisation itself has become increasingly fragmented.

The division

The state has not succeeded in producing a decisive split in PTI through defections. The party has nevertheless experienced substantial organic internal division. Imran Khan’s family, ideological loyalists, pragmatists, provincial politicians and competing organisational factions have struggled to establish authority in his absence. They have not had the discipline for their disagreements not to become public, weakening the possibility of a coherent alternative strategy.

The only strategy capable of commanding broad agreement has often been the one Imran Khan pursued when he was free. But that strategy was developed in a different political environment, when PTI enjoyed greater institutional access and faced a state whose response to political mobilisation was less restrictive.

The party has also overestimated the practical importance of international support. Expectations that foreign governments, including a returning Donald Trump administration, might intervene decisively on Khan’s behalf were never a substitute for domestic political negotiation.

The diaspora has presented another complication. Overseas PTI supporters have sustained the party’s international visibility and political messaging, but sections of its external support base have also resisted compromises that might appear insufficiently loyal to Khan. Those living outside Pakistan do not necessarily bear the same immediate costs as party workers, officeholders and families confronting the state at home.

This is not an argument against the diaspora’s political participation. It is an argument about the consequences of allowing those least exposed to the costs of confrontation to exercise disproportionate influence over the terms of compromise.

In KP, these pressures contributed to an increasingly confrontational political vocabulary. References to Bangladesh’s history, suggestions that the provincial budget might be withheld to produce a constitutional crisis, and proposals involving direct engagement with Afghanistan all raised the stakes.

Some of these ideas were unlikely to be carried through, they were the bluster of maximalist rhetoric aimed at eliciting pressure. That did not make them harmless though, especially the threat of a province conducting its own foreign policy as soverign. They made it easier for the federal government to see provincial dissent as a challenge to the constitutional order, even when the underlying disagreement was milder than the rhetoric.

The clearest example is the controversy over counterterrorism operations in the former tribal areas.

Opposition to another major military operation should not automatically be interpreted as sympathy for militants. Communities in the merged districts have lived through displacement, the destruction of homes and livelihoods, and the prolonged uncertainty of returning to places that had ceased to resemble the homes they left.

Their demand to be consulted before another operation is grounded in that experience. For families who have already lost homes, businesses and years of ordinary life, assurances that displacement will be temporary are no longer sufficient. Many residents also question the durability of earlier security gains, particularly when militant activity subsequently returned to areas that had been cleared at enormous human cost by inviting them back.

PTI has not always articulated these concerns effectively when they conflated these with demands of the release of Imran Khan. This unfortunately obscured the legitimate demands of the population it represents. But the underlying argument deserves to be taken seriously: a security operation that depends on the cooperation of local communities cannot treat their fears as evidence of disloyalty.

A dangerous neighbourhood

Pakistan is operating in a more dangerous neighbourhood than it was when PTI first assumed power in KP in 2013. The military confrontation with India in May 2025 demonstrated how quickly a terrorist attack and subsequent military retaliation could escalate into direct conflict between two nuclear-armed states. The crisis involved strikes against military targets and created risks that extended well beyond the immediate battlefield.

To the west, relations with Afghanistan have deteriorated from uneasy coexistence into recurring military confrontation. Pakistan has carried out cross-border strikes against what it identifies as militant sanctuaries. These disputes have produced armed exchanges, disrupted border communities and further complicated the security situation in KP.

The wider Middle East adds another layer of uncertainty. Israel’s expanding regional confrontations and its security relationships with India are relevant to Pakistan’s strategic calculations, particularly when viewed against Pakistan’s established diplomatic position on Palestine. In such circumstances, effective coordination between federal and provincial authorities becomes more important, while political confrontation makes that coordination harder. But is this a legitimate canvass for an emergency?

The federal government cannot expect unquestioning provincial compliance merely by invoking national security. The provincial government cannot treat every security initiative as an extension of its political dispute with Islamabad. Both have obligations that extend beyond their immediate political interests.

PTI’s failure to build broader coalitions has made this confrontation more difficult to manage. The party has historically preferred strategies that demonstrate the moral certainty of its position, including electoral boycotts and resignations, even when those decisions have weakened its institutional influence. In the present circumstances, coalition-building was arguably more valuable than another attempt to occupy D-Chowk. A PTI whose street mobilisation had weakened needed the support of parties such as JUI-F and other political actors capable of broadening the dispute beyond the fate of Imran Khan.

This loss of the street made keeping the provincial government exceptionally important. Even as its national mobilisation capacity weakened, PTI retained the administrative and political resources of KP. The chief minister’s office gave it visibility, authority and the ability to sustain political activity that an opposition party operating without provincial power would find much harder to organise.

The distinction between legitimate government activity and partisan mobilisation therefore became increasingly contested. Orders by the Peshawar and Islamabad High Courts restricting the use of public resources for political protests reduced the room for treating provincial administrative machinery as an extension of party organisation.

The pressure was no longer confined to political leaders. Civil servants and police officers faced increasingly explicit expectations that they should not facilitate partisan protests through official resources. This mattered because the institutional advantages of holding provincial office were becoming more difficult to deploy. A mobilisation that could be restricted within KP itself would face considerable difficulties reaching Islamabad.

The trigger

So why has the Federal Government finally pulled the trigger? Security deterioration supplied the stated constitutional justification. The confrontation over provincial authority, political mobilisation and the limits of federal tolerance supplied its immediate political context. The decision has now changed the incentives for everyone involved.

PTI has lost its provincial government, but the federal authorities have also relieved it of the immediate responsibility of governing KP. This is the central paradox of the intervention.

For years, PTI had to reconcile its position as a party of confrontation with its obligations as the government of a province facing terrorism, fiscal constraints and difficult relations with the federation. Its opponents could point to failures in policing, administration and economic management. PTI could blame Islamabad, but it could not entirely escape responsibility for the province it governed – such are the dangers of incumbency. Now Governor’s rule changes that calculation.

The federal government and the establishment now assume a much greater share of responsibility for what happens in KP. They have reduced PTI’s ability to use the provincial government as an instrument of political mobilisation, but they have also reduced the extent to which PTI can be held directly accountable for provincial administration during the intervention.

Every administrative failure, disruption in services or deterioration in security risks becoming an argument against the intervention. Every improvement, meanwhile, will be claimed by the federal authorities as evidence that their decision was necessary. PTI does not need to demonstrate that it could govern better under the new arrangement. It needs to persuade its supporters that the elected government was displaced and that the federal authorities have failed to justify the consequences.

The asymmetry is important. The federal government faces a considerably more demanding test. It must demonstrate that extraordinary constitutional intervention can deliver results that ordinary provincial government could not. That means improvements in security, administrative performance and the everyday conditions of people living in KP. It must also demonstrate that the intervention is constitutionally defensible and proportionate to the circumstances that prompted it.

Success in administration would strengthen the political argument for the decision. It would not, by itself, settle the constitutional question. An intervention cannot acquire legality retrospectively merely because some of its outcomes are favourable. Nor can political success be measured solely by the restoration of order in Islamabad. Preventing another march on D-Chowk may address an immediate federal concern, but it does little to resolve the insecurity of communities in southern KP or the governance challenges confronting the province.

Recent political history offers a warning about the burden of raised expectations. After Imran Khan’s removal in 2022, supporters of the succeeding political arrangement expected a more competent management of the economy. The caretaker period that followed did not produce the transformation many had anticipated. Economic conditions remained difficult, and the political cost of unmet expectations was substantial. The same danger now confronts those assuming responsibility for KP.

PTI’s record in the province stretches back to 2013. It has had ample opportunity to establish its own standards of governance, and its performance deserves scrutiny. But replacing an elected government through extraordinary constitutional measures raises expectations that the replacement arrangement will achieve something demonstrably better.

That is an exceptionally demanding proposition in a province facing persistent militancy, displacement, unemployment, fiscal dependence and difficult terrain. It is also a proposition that cannot be fulfilled by security measures alone. A durable improvement would require political legitimacy, functioning civilian institutions and a relationship with local communities that extends beyond the demands of counterterrorism.

The possibility of renewed protest remains. Removing PTI from provincial office may strengthen its account of political exclusion and give its supporters a grievance around which to organise. Whether that produces sustained mobilisation is uncertain. The disappointments of 2024 have not disappeared, and the willingness to vote for PTI should not be mistaken for a willingness to participate in another confrontation.

But the removal of governmental responsibility changes the party’s incentives. PTI may find it easier to reject compromises when it no longer bears the immediate costs of administering the province. The federal government may therefore discover that it has constrained one source of PTI’s power while strengthening another source of its political appeal.

Constitutionally, governor’s rule under Article 234 is limited to six months, with parliamentary approval required for its continuation within that period. The simultaneous invocation of Article 232 creates a more complicated legal situation, but it does not automatically eliminate the limitations attached to Article 234. Any attempt to prolong extraordinary federal control would have to confront those distinctions.

PTI consequently retains several possible courses of action. It can challenge the intervention in court, attempt to mobilise opposition through protests, or negotiate a new political arrangement that preserves its long-term position while accepting the limits of its immediate power. None of these is without difficulty.

Legal proceedings may be prolonged or unsuccessful. Street protests may fail to achieve their objectives while imposing further costs on supporters. Negotiation would require a willingness to accept outcomes short of PTI’s maximal demands, and a party whose internal factions disagree over the meaning of compromise may struggle to sustain such an approach.

The federal authorities face choices of their own. If the intervention fails to achieve its stated objectives, they may seek to extend extraordinary measures or consider further restrictions on PTI, including renewed efforts to prohibit the party’s activities. Such measures would introduce additional legal, political and polarisation risks.

There is also an external dimension in these tough times. In a country already exposed to confrontation with India and instability along the Afghan border, prolonged internal political exclusion can create opportunities for hostile actors to exploit public grievances. To be clear, that is a risk to be assessed, not a licence to attribute domestic dissent to foreign sponsorship.

The deeper question is whether Pakistan’s political institutions can still produce a negotiated settlement between parties that increasingly regard compromise as surrender. For PTI, the challenge is to recognise that electoral popularity does not confer unlimited bargaining power because that is poor strategy which is not serving them well anymore given how much is stacked against it, and that preserving a political movement may require a different strategy from the one that sustained it during Imran Khan’s years in opposition.

For the federal government and establishment, the challenge is to recognise that administrative control does not necessarily suppress a mobilisation does not settle the grievances from which it emerged. Both sides have repeatedly demonstrated an ability to impose costs on the other. Neither has yet demonstrated a convincing ability to end the confrontation. But Governor’s rule changes the distribution of those costs. It also changes the burden of accountability.

PTI has lost the government it regarded as its last institutional stronghold. The federal authorities have acquired direct responsibility for a province whose difficulties are unlikely to yield to extraordinary powers alone.

The next six months will test the proposition that federal control can succeed where elected provincial government was judged to have failed. The result will depend on measurable outcomes, the legality of the intervention and the ability to restore a functioning political relationship. Unfortunately, in Pakistan, a mandate, power or success have never been entirely synonymous. What’s changed now is that the federal government is willing to impose enhanced costs on the PTI – and it’s unlikely to stop here because PTI’s electoral strength, organisational capacity and ability to mobilise protesters are no longer necessarily moving in tandem. The federal government has taken away the PTI’s power, but also taken away their reasons for restraint while burdening the new government with extraordinary expectations of delivery to justify the use of emergency provisions.

Houthi forces warn against use of Saudi airports following Riyadh attack

Submitted by Fleur Hargreaves on Sun, 10/11/2026 - 13:56
Warning comes one day after an alleged Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport forced authorities to halt operations
Military spokesman of Yemen's Houthi group Yahya Saree addresses a Palestine solidarity rally in the capital Sanaa on 2 May 2025 (Mohammed Huwais/AFP)
Off

Yemen’s Houthis have delivered renewed warnings to stay away from all Saudi airports except Mecca and Medina, one day after an alleged Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital city of Riyadh.

In a post on X on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree warned all shipping companies, airlines, employees and travellers against using airports in Saudi Arabia.

“The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of Mecca and Medina,” he added, referring to the two holiest cities in Islam.

Saree urged “everyone to take our warnings seriously” and said Saudi Arabia “bore responsibility for failed interceptions” of the attack.

Authorities suspended operations at the airport until 21:00 GMT on Sunday, according to a Notice to Air Missions (Notam) issued by Saudi civil aviation authorities, after the attack killed 12 and injured more than 300 others in the deadliest strike on the kingdom for more than a decade.

The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said in a statement on Sunday that four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese had been killed in the attack late on Saturday.

Kuwait Airways announced the cancellation of two flights scheduled to and from Riyadh on Sunday due to what it describes as a “temporary suspension of operations” from the Saudi authorities.

International reaction

While the Houthis have not claimed responsibility for the strike, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen attributed it to them, calling it a “full-fledged war crime”. 

Several other regional and international nations have condemned the attack, including Iraq, the UAE, Qatar, Germany, France and Britain, as well as European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen and United Nations General Secretary Antonio Guterres.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called the attack “contemptible” and a “dangerous escalation”, saying it explains “one of the reasons why the UK is providing support to Saudi Arabia in the form of air defences but also air-to-air refuelling” in an interview with Sky News on Sunday.

When asked if the UK’s support for the kingdom could go further, Streeting told the BBC that “potentially” it could. 

The airport has faced repeated targeting from the Yemeni armed group, but this alleged attack would mark the most deadly escalation in their “tit-for-tat” strikes with the neighbouring Gulf state. 

Houthi-affiliated media reported on Friday that Saudi strikes on the airport in the Houthi-controlled capital city of Sanaa killed two people, a day after their attacks against Riyadh airport killed three. 

Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government have launched repeated strikes across Yemen, hitting civilian infrastructure, including airports, but this has not prohibited the Yemeni group from being able to launch missiles and drones back at the kingdom.

EU warned that strikes by "Iran’s proxies" risk pushing the region into a wider cycle of violence.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the attack as a “dangerous escalation” and called on the Houthis to stop targeting civilian infrastructure.

“These attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwaves sent through the world. These murderous attacks on civilians must stop at once,” the EU chief wrote on X on Sunday.

She added that the EU stood in “solidarity with Saudi Arabia”.

The Saudi-led coalition blamed Yemen’s Houthi movement for the Saturday attack, describing it as a “full-fledged war crime”.

Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement that four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed in the attack.

item.title: Houthi strike on Riyadh airport kills 12; Saudi-led coalition vows 'decisive' response to worst attack on kingdom in a decade
item.description:
At least 12 people were killed and more than 300 wounded in an attack on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade, as the Houthis escalate a campaign they launched this summer.

The dead from the third attack this week on the airport included four Saudis, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. At the latest count, 309 were wounded, officials said.

While the Houthis stopped short of claiming the strike, they threatened new attacks on the kingdom’s airports, except for the holy cities of Makkah and Madina, warning passengers not to travel.

“The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces,” military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X.

President Donald Trump said Washington was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the war on Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.

Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, some in critical condition after the attack, which occurred without warning.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the Houthi attack on Sunday, reiterating Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi Arabia’s security under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen blamed the group for the strike on King Khalid International Airport, describing it as a “full-fledged war crime” that a diplomatic source attributed to a missile.

Earlier in the day, authorities had suspended operations at Riyadh’s international airport. The Saudi civil aviation authority had initially confirmed an attack had injured several people at the sprawling King Khalid International Airport, with a diplomatic source attributing it to a missile fired by Yemen’s Houthi rebels.

The situation prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the “serious emergency”, a medical source said, while foreign embassies warned their citizens to avoid the facility.

Houthis have repeatedly targeted the facility, claiming a series of strikes on Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not announce any new attacks on Saturday.

Air traffic monitor Flightradar24 said 155 arriving and 161 departing flights had been cancelled, while a total of 222 flights were delayed.

At around 6pm local time, Flightradar24 noted that flights bound for the airport were “diverting elsewhere, mainly to Jeddah at the moment”. It later shared a notice to airmen (Notam) for operations suspended till 12am.

A witness at the airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded and fleeing in panic.

“I was on gate 403” at the domestic terminal, the witness told AFP. “I saw 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”

A medical source told AFP that the health ministry had ordered ER doctors to report to hospitals around the capital to treat the wounded on Saturday.

“We were told we are dealing with a ‘serious emergency situation’. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh”, with many in critical condition, the source said.

The aviation authority said the number of injured from the attack was still being assessed, adding that airport “operations had been temporarily suspended pending the completion of an assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities”.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s coalition government unravelled in July.

A source at a local hospital said five people were in intensive care there after being wounded at the airport, with “dozens of people injured” in all.

A relative of one wounded person said they had been hit in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass. Three witnesses confirmed people being evacuated from the airport.

Two doctors told AFP that several pilgrims headed to Makkah had been injured while waiting to board their flight.

A diplomatic source briefed on the matter told AFP the airport was hit by “a missile around 3:00pm” (5pm PKT).

“Houthis are attacking civilian targets. Riyadh airport is a civilian target,” the source said.

‘War crime’

The Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Malki described the strike as a “cowardly terrorist attack” against a civilian facility.

“The cowardly terrorist attack by the terrorist Houthi militia… which resulted in deaths and injuries among civilian passengers and airport staff, constitutes a full-fledged war crime,” he said in a statement on X.

US ‘may’ join Saudi strikes

Asked on Saturday whether he had changed his mind about joining Saudi strikes on the group, US President Donald Trump said: “We may.”

He said he would be speaking with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, calling what happened in Saudi Arabia “not acceptable”.

US media outlets have reported that previous Saudi requests for US military assistance in dealing with the Houthis have been rebuffed.

Embassy warnings

The Yemen conflict flared back to life after a four-year, UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle Eastern war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.

The scale and frequency of the recent strikes targeting Riyadh are unprecedented in the eight months of war in the region.

Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that supports Yemen’s government militarily, and has found itself drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbour’s civil war.

Both Riyadh and the Houthis have signalled a willingness to keep fighting rather than pursue diplomacy.

The US embassy in Saudi Arabia said it was “aware of attacks” on Riyadh airport on Saturday and called on American citizens to avoid the area.

The Canadian, German and Spanish embassies also warned their citizens to avoid the facility. Spain’s embassy, in a message on X, alerted nationals to a “new attack… by the Houthis”.

A senior Western diplomat told AFP that several embassies “indicated that they had decided to prohibit their staff’s travel to/from Riyadh Airport over the next week as a prudential step”.

Near the airport, passengers carrying luggage could be seen standing on the pavement at a metro station.

Yemen fighting

Meanwhile, in Yemen, Saudi-led government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas they captured last month around the Bab al-Mandab strait, military sources told AFP.

The Yemeni government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, after the group seized the country’s entire western coastline in a lightning offensive.

The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandab area — a key chokepoint for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping — but they claimed to have repelled the assault.

Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

item.title: Experiment or stick with the winning XI? Pakistan face selection dilemma ahead of second Sri Lanka T20I
item.description:
Pakistan will meet Sri Lanka on Sunday evening for the second of a three-match Twenty20 international series, where the Green Shirts will look to take an unassailable 2-0 lead and seal the series.

Pakistan’s standout performers, Maaz Sadaqat and skipper Sahibzada Farhan will look to replicate their respective strong outings from Friday, with both declaring their commitment to playing their natural game in a way that the modern format demands.

In the post-match press conference after the first match on Friday, top-order batter Maaz said that he planned on backing his natural game and play the way he has been playing,

Pakistan beat Sri Lanka by four wickets, accomplished with a largely untroubled chase of the 183-run target which they achieved with seven balls remaining, despite a cluster of wickets falling at the toe-end of the innings.

“It was my first 50 so I am very happy,” said Maaz, who scored a maiden, blistering T20 international half-century off 26 balls at one-drop. “The plan for upcoming matches is to play the way I have been playing and back it.”

Maaz’s rich vein of form can be traced back to last month’s Caribbean Premiere League (CPL), where he scored 363 runs in seven matches at a strike rate of almost 175. His campaign also included two centuries, one of which came in the competition’s final.

In the second match of the series, Maaz can potentially cement his spot in the side further. It could also be interesting to note whether Maaz remains at one-drop, or if Pakistan want to test him as an opener.

Maaz himself believes the two positions are interchangeable, which he said whilst answering a question about whether taking over the position Babar Azam normally played in was a source of extra pressure.

“I am comfortable in this position, but for Pakistan I am prepared to bat at any position,” he said.

Farhan, too, backed Maaz.

“I think, the sort of form Maaz is in, he is one of the best players,” he said after the first match.

“I told him to take advantage of his current form,” he said, adding that he was “very happy” as his captain.

“Today I told him, now that you have the opportunity, you should complete your 50. If you complete your 5o, we can finish this match three or four overs earlier,” Farhan later told the broadcaster in the post-match show.

The skipper was named player of the match himself for his 53-ball-89, in his third match as T20I captain following the two matches that were part of the team’s silver-winning Asian Games campaign.

He added that he had changed the way he played over the last year to strike at at least 150-160 instead of the lower strike rates he used to record before, because such is the demand of the modern game.

Echoing Maaz’s sentiment, he added that he will continue to bat the way he has been batting and not change it as long as the game demanded it, “whether I am captain or not.”

The series is his first assignment at home as captain, and its outcome and findings could be formative for a Pakistan T20 side that is somewhat in the process of a re-build, with senior mainstays like Babar Azam, Mohammad Rizwan and Shaheen Afridi not currently part of the squad. It provides an opportunity for the management and the new skipper to further assess team combinations and line-ups.

“It would be a lie to say there is no pressure, because when you are representing your country, people have expectations from you,” the captain said.

‘‘As a captain, I am very happy with this team… (In T20s) I think three or four boys perform and it is enough to turn the tables in a match.”

“If you look at it, we have Arafat Minhas as a backup. We have Abdul Samad, Sufiyan Muqeem. So, our back-up strength is very strong,” he said, adding that this bench strength also meant that the playing combinations were not fixed and that they could always experiment and change in upcoming matches.

Whether Pakistan chooses to actually test the strength of its bench could be another interesting element to look out for, going into this second match.

All of them have made a case for themselves: Arafat bowled a disciplined spell of 2-23 in three overs in the Asian Games semi-final. And though not in the same format, he has already starred in the greens, picking up a Player of the Series award in his debut One-day International series against Australia earlier this year.

Abdul Samad’s clinical 15-ball-30 against Bangladesh played a starring role in the team reaching the gold-medal match in the Asian Games.

And while Sufiyan’s returns against India were not entirely prodigal, he is still coming off the back of a T20 season that saw him named Player of the Tournament in Peshawar Zalmi’s Pakistan Super League title-winning run and, more recently, be named Player of the Final in the CPL for a record spell of 4-14.

Pakistan’s previous T20 sides were often criticised for not using bilateral fixtures to amply experiment and give match time to young players, focusing too much on the results as opposed to the long-term process.

Maaz, for example, was asked in the press conference whether Shadab Khan was occupying a space that could potentially have gone to a younger player (to which his response was simple: “He was selected on merit.”)

Whether Pakistan seek to play a fresher XI tonight, or chooses to not fix what was not broken in the first match, remains to be seen.

New date announced for cancelled Department of Youth Development recruitment test
item.description:
The recruitment test for assistant upazila youth development officers under the Department of Youth Development, which was cancelled over allegations of a question paper leak, will be held on Friday, 16 October.

The one-hour examination will take place from 3:00 pm to 4:00 pm that day. DM Atikur Rahman, director (administration) of the Department of Youth Development, confirmed the information.

Meanwhile, the Ministry of Youth and Sports has formed a five-member committee to investigate the allegations. The committee has been asked to submit its report within the next three working days.

Around 300,000 jobseekers applied for the recruitment test for 242 posts. They travelled to Dhaka to sit the examination today, Saturday, only to learn at the last moment that it had been cancelled.

As a result, they faced various difficulties, including travel, accommodation and food expenses. After the cancellation was announced, angry candidates staged spontaneous protests on roads in different parts of Dhaka. Some also demanded compensation.

Job exam scraped at last minute, 300,000 aspirants seek compensation

Cancellation announced after OMR sheets distributed

The recruitment test for assistant upazila youth development officers was scheduled to take place today, Saturday. Candidates travelled to Dhaka from different parts of the country. About two minutes after OMR sheets were distributed at the examination centres, they were informed that the test had been cancelled.

Faria Ferdous, a student at MM College in Jashore, had travelled to Dhaka to sit the examination. She said the cancellation was announced immediately after the OMR sheets were distributed at the centre. They had not expected to face such a situation after travelling from distant places with their preparations complete, she said.

After news of the cancellation spread, candidates staged spontaneous protests on roads in different parts of Dhaka, including Motijheel, Manik Mia Avenue and Sat Masjid Road.

Their main grievance was that the decision to cancel the examination had been communicated only after they reached the centres. In addition to their exam preparations, the money they had spent on travelling to Dhaka, accommodation and food had consequently become an uncertain loss.

A candidate from the Department of Physics at Khulna University of Engineering and Technology said nearly 300,000 jobseekers had travelled to Dhaka to sit the examination. He questioned who would bear their travel, accommodation and food expenses. Some candidates demanded compensation.

Allegations of question paper leak

The night before the examination, allegations emerged that the question paper had been circulated on social media. Candidates alleged that although there had been discussions about the circulation of the question paper beforehand, the decision to cancel the examination was announced only after they had reached the centres.

This further increased the difficulties faced by candidates who had travelled from distant places.

DM Atikur Rahman, director (administration) of the Department of Youth Development, had said that some parts of the questions circulated on social media matched those in the actual question paper. The decision to cancel the examination was taken for this reason.

After the cancellation, candidates had been waiting for a new date to be announced. According to sources at the department, the examination will now be held on Friday, 16 October, from 3:00 pm to 4:00 pm.

Candidates will therefore have to prepare for the examination again. Those who travelled to Dhaka from different districts and faced difficulties the previous day will have to make travel arrangements once more to sit the examination on the new date.

Nearly 300,000 applications for 242 posts

The post of assistant upazila youth development officer is in the 11th grade of government service. A recruitment notice was published to fill 242 posts, attracting around 300,000 applicants. This means an average of approximately 1,240 candidates are competing for each post.

Intense competition for government jobs in the employment market makes recruitment examinations extremely important for candidates. Many spend money on preparation, travel and accommodation. As a result, cancellation of an examination causes not only financial losses but also a waste of their time and preparation.

According to World Bank estimates for 2025, around two million young people enter Bangladesh’s labour market each year. With so many young people seeking employment, competition for the limited number of government jobs has become increasingly intense.

The announcement of a new date has now given candidates another opportunity to sit the examination. However, no information was available on whether the department had decided to compensate candidates for the difficulties they faced the previous day.

Investigation committee formed

A press release issued today by the office of the director general of the Department of Youth Development said a five-member committee had been formed to investigate the allegations of a question paper leak. The additional secretary of the administration wing of the Ministry of Youth and Sports has been appointed as convener of the committee.

The other members are a joint secretary from the relevant section of the Ministry of Youth and Sports, a representative of joint secretary rank from the Ministry of Public Administration, and a director of the Department of Youth Development. The department’s deputy director (administration sub-division) will serve as member-secretary.

The office order states that the committee must investigate the circulation of the recruitment examination’s question paper on social media and submit its report within the next three working days. The committee may co-opt new members if necessary. Disciplinary action will be taken against those found responsible after the investigation report is received.

item.title: PM assures support for waste-to-fuel technology
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday assured support for a technology that could turn waste into fuel oil and help reduce Bangladesh’s dependence on imported energy.
He gave the assurance as a team of researchers led by Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (Kuet) Professor Dr Md Khalequzzaman briefed him on the technology at his office in Tejgaon, said a release issued by the PM’s Press Wing.
The technology uses a process known as hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) to convert human waste, waste from sewage treatment plants, kitchen waste and agricultural residues into fuel oil.
The researchers said they have been working on the technology for around 10 years and have achieved a 50–55% biocrude yield in laboratory tests. They have also made progress in producing biocrude with a high diesel content.
The next step is to set up a pilot plant capable of processing one to three tons of waste daily to assess the technology’s efficiency, production costs and commercial viability. The estimated cost of the pilot project is Tk100–120 crore.
According to the researchers, the technology, if developed for commercial-scale production, could replace around 10–15% of imported crude oil and save foreign currency equivalent to Tk6,500–13,000 crore annually.
However, the estimates would need to be validated through large-scale technical and economic assessments, they said.
The researchers said the technology could also help reduce environmental pollution, improve waste management and create opportunities for developing a domestic fuel industry.
The Prime Minister assured them of the government’s necessary cooperation in advancing the initiative.
Power and Energy Minister Iqbal Mahmood Tuku, State Minister Anindya Islam Amit, University Grants Commission member Professor Abdullah Al Mamun, Kuet Vice-Chancellor Professor Mohammad Masud and Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation Chairman Dr Mohammad Rafiqul Islam were present at the briefing.

item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir on Saturday said Bangladesh was positively considering the Makkah Defence Agreement, with any decision to be guided by national interests and the potential contribution of the country's peacekeeping expertise to regional peace and stability.
“We are having positive discussions on the Makkah Defence Agreement. We are viewing it positively,” he said while addressing a national seminar at the Foreign Service Academy in the capital.
Kobir said Bangladesh could take a favourable decision if the agreement served its national interests and its peacekeeping expertise could contribute to the welfare of Muslim nations and help maintain peace and stability in the Middle East.
“If it falls within the national interests of Bangladesh and converges, and we feel that our peacekeeping expertise can add value in serving Muslim nations and keeping a stable, peaceful Middle East, then there is every scope to take a positive decision on the matter,” he said.
The Bangladesh Institute of International and Strategic Studies (BIISS) and the Center for Migration Studies of North South University (NSU) jointly organised the seminar titled “From Workforce to Strategic Partnership: Reimagining Bangladesh-KSA Relations.”
The state minister also said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had accepted an invitation from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince to visit the Kingdom.
“He has accepted and will do so at some point very soon,” Kobir said.
He said the Crown Prince had also expressed interest in visiting Bangladesh, adding that Dhaka would welcome him at a mutually convenient time.
Kobir said the proposed visits reflected growing political ties between the two countries. He also described Bangladesh as a strong partner of Saudi Arabia in maritime security.
Calling for a comprehensive economic and strategic partnership, he said bilateral relations should expand beyond their traditional focus on labour migration and remittances.
“While that foundation remains important, it cannot be the ceiling of our ambition,” he said.
He said Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 and Bangladesh's economic transformation had created common interests in investment, human capital, technology and connectivity.
Discussions were underway on a possible investment fund to facilitate joint investments and partnerships in priority sectors, he added.
The state minister identified renewable energy, infrastructure, ports, logistics, agriculture, fisheries, food security, healthcare, pharmaceuticals, information technology and artificial intelligence as promising areas for Saudi investment.
He said such investments required a predictable and transparent business environment, improved institutional coordination and timely decision-making.
Kobir stressed the need to shift towards trained and certified professionals to meet the changing demands of Saudi Arabia's labour market.
He called for stronger cooperation among training institutions, universities and industries to ensure skills certification aligned with Saudi market requirements.
The welfare, dignity and rights of Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia would remain a government priority, he said.
Kobir also highlighted opportunities for knowledge and technology partnerships, alongside cooperation in ports, shipping, logistics, aviation and supply chains.
“The next chapter of Bangladesh-Saudi Arabia relations should therefore be defined by value creation rather than volume alone,” he said.
Saudi Arabia’s Ambassador to Bangladesh Dr Abdullah Zafer bin Abiyah addressed the seminar as the guest of honour. Foreign Ministry Secretary (Bilateral) Dr Md Nazrul Islam and Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Secretary Md Mokhtar Ahmed spoke as special guests.
BIISS Director General Major General A S M Ridwanur Rahman and NSU Vice-Chancellor Professor Abdul Hannan Chowdhury also addressed the seminar.
Speaking to journalists after the event, Kobir reiterated that peace and stability in the Middle East and the Muslim world were central to Bangladesh's consideration of the Makkah Defence Agreement.
He said maintaining peace in the region encompassing Makkah and Madinah was a key objective, adding that Bangladesh could deploy its peacekeeping expertise more effectively and extensively across the world.
He said initiatives regarding participation in the agreement or association with the alliance were being considered positively, with regional peace and stability remaining the priority.
Kobir said regular high-level exchanges, including ministerial and official visits in both directions, were strengthening bilateral engagement.
He also stressed the need to diversify employment opportunities into energy, technology and other promising sectors while sending more highly skilled professionals to Saudi Arabia.
“We are also holding very positive discussions with Saudi Arabia and, God willing, many new opportunities will emerge between the two countries,” he said.
The state minister said there was scope for a broad investment partnership under which Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia could jointly invest in profitable sectors.
“The days of dependency are over. We are now placing emphasis on an equal partnership between the two countries and on sustainable policies,” he told journalists.

item.title: Brazil’s Lula scraps gasoline tax ahead of runoff election
item.description:
Brazil’s government announced on Friday that gasoline taxes will be temporarily scrapped, two weeks ahead of the runoff election between incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro.
Lula, who is seeking his fourth term, is trying to contain rising fuel prices amid a global spike in oil prices driven by the war in the Middle East.
The gasoline tax, which was set at 0.89 reais ($0.18) per liter, would be waived for 30 days, according to the government.
The measure announced on Friday also expands subsidies for importers of diesel, the predominant fuel used in Brazil’s freight transport.
“The objective is to ensure that imports remain viable at a critical moment for supply,” the presidency said in a statement.
The fiscal impact of the tax exemptions will be offset by Brazil’s “extraordinary revenues” from oil exports, it said.
The runoff election on October 25 was set after Lula won 45% of the vote in the first round and Bolsonaro received 47%.
Bolsonaro called his opponent “irresponsible,” warning that Lula was placing a “bomb” on consumers’ laps and that diesel prices could rise after the election.
Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, repeatedly criticized the government during his campaign for failing to control the cost of living.
Inflation in Brazil rose by 0.82% in September, the statistics authority said on Friday.

item.title: Trump, Putin reach deal to release Russian diesel to world
item.description:
US President Donald Trump on Friday said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release Russian diesel to US and global markets.
The move, which aims to address rising fuel costs before the US midterm elections, marks a dramatic turnaround in US policy toward Moscow since the start of the war in Ukraine.
In a social media post, Trump wrote he had made a deal with Putin during a phone call that was supposed to be about a suspected plague outbreak in Russia.
According to Trump, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.”
Trump wrote that Russia would deliver another 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that.
The US Treasury Department issued a temporary license that will allow Russian diesel to reach global markets through April 2027.
Trump’s announcement follows his signing of a broad Russia sanctions law last month. The law is intended to clamp down on Russia’s energy sector and other areas that fuel its war against Ukraine.
Kirill Dmitriev, the Russian presidential envoy, reposted the Treasury Department’s announcement on X, saying that “Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world.”
Alexander Novak, Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister, said that the country was ready to start supplying additional volumes of diesel to the United States and other countries from October.
He also said that Russia’s exports are expected to rise further in November and December as refineries resume operations after maintenance.
Later, the Kremlin released a statement from Putin saying that, during their call, he and Trump had also devoted “significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis” and had discussed “the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned the agreement, saying that any easing of sanctions without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious sign of “weakness.”
“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy,” he wrote on social media.
“Allowing Russia to ⁠sell ​petroleum products ​is an investment in a ​war that ‌must be ended, not prolonged. What ​is needed ⁠is real de-escalation with Russia ⁠on ​a reciprocal basis,” the Ukrainian president stressed.
Zelensky added that Ukraine hopes the US will have a strong conversation with Russia: “A strong one, not a weak one.”
Since its 2022 full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine, Moscow has been hit with rounds of sanctions by the United States and its Western partners.
But as the war has continued with no resolution in sight, Washington’s commitment to that approach has appeared to waver.
Earlier this year, temporary US sanctions waivers that allowed the sale of Russian oil raised concerns because they could hinder efforts to deprive Moscow of funds for its war in Ukraine.
Last month, Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for soaring diesel prices, and even publicly told Zelensky to stop the attacks.
Trump’s announcement on Friday came just as US, Ukrainian, and European officials were meeting in Miami for new diplomatic talks aimed at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine.

item.title: Abdul Awal Mintoo: Bangladesh, India to hold talks on elephant corridor in Sherpur
item.description:
Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo on Saturday said the government would soon initiate talks with India under an existing protocol to establish a cross-border corridor for wild elephants roaming the Garo Hills in Sherpur.
Around 130 to 135 wild elephants that came from India's Meghalaya have become stranded in the Garo Hills of Sherpur as border fencing has prevented them from returning to their habitat, he said.
The minister said the government would request the Indian authorities to open gates in the fencing to allow the elephants to return, although previous requests had not received a positive response.
At the same time, initiatives would be taken to develop forest areas in Sherpur into safe habitats for the elephants, he added.
The minister made the remarks while speaking at a discussion on resolving human-elephant conflict and conserving wild elephants at Madhutila Eco Park in Nalitabari upazila of Sherpur.
He said the scenic Garo Hills, its wild elephants and the surrounding natural environment would be used to develop the area into a tourism hub. This would create economic opportunities for local people while helping protect elephants and reduce human-elephant conflict, he added.
The Sherpur district administration and the Mymensingh Forest Division organized the discussion with lawmakers from elephant-affected areas, Elephant Response Team (ERT) members, journalists and volunteers involved in elephant conservation. Deputy Commissioner Farida Yesmin chaired the event.
Sherpur-2 lawmaker Engineer Fahim Chowdhury, Chief Conservator of Forests Md Amir Hossain Chowdhury, Conservator of Forests for the Wildlife and Nature Conservation Region Md Sanaullah Patwari, Central Region Conservator of Forests ASM Zahir Uddin Akon, Mymensingh Divisional Forest Officer Kazi Muhammad Nurul Karim and Police Superintendent AKM Johirul Islam spoke as special guests.
